# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up does the right things. It:

- registers its mediation test before the 24-month data existed,
- adds a stricter hours measure (system logs) to check for unrecorded work,
- answers both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis with evidence rather than assertion, and
- labels the Halden subset clearly as survivors.

The headline arithmetic checks out:

- **Timesheet hours:** 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% per hour.
- **Log hours:** 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5% per hour.
- **Halden subset:** 0.968/0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares** sum to 100%.

The problems are mostly about interpretation, and one of them affects the decay finding directly. Most important first.

## 1. The control group was contaminated, which affects the decay finding

In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit" and cut meeting time from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. Their output per hour then rose by 4.1%. The paper treats this as an interesting side observation. It is also a **contamination of the comparison group**, and it biases the 24-month difference-in-differences toward zero.

- **Rough size:** a 4.1% gain in 2 of 7 control offices raises the control mean by about 1.2 points. That is a substantial share of the 2.7-point "decline" from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- **So part of the apparent fading may be the control group catching up**, not the treated offices' gain decaying. The paper's novelty-consistent reading ("some fading of an initial effect") is only one explanation.
- **The audit itself may be spillover.** Control offices in the same county probably heard what the treated offices were doing about meetings. If so, the trial is partly testing the diffusion of the intervention.

Needed:

- treated and control trajectories reported separately;
- a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audited offices, or censoring them at month 15;
- softer wording on decay until those are shown.

## 2. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms"

- **The effective sample size is 14 offices.** Treatment was randomised at office level, and the mediators vary mainly between offices. A "larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measures, not independent units. A 95% CI of 28–66% for an indirect effect identified from 14 clusters looks too narrow. Please confirm that the standard errors account for clustering, e.g. with a cluster bootstrap.
- **It tests the hypothesis on the same units that suggested it.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices. A registered test on the same offices, using data that overlaps the exploratory period, is better than nothing, but it is not an independent replication. A cleaner confirmatory test would use only post-registration data (months 12–24).
- **Mediation requires no unmeasured confounding between the mediators and the outcome.** Offices whose managers cut meetings may differ in other ways, such as management quality. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary's "confirms" should then be "supports."
- **Where did the baseline data come from?** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected *only in month six*. This report gives baseline meeting figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). If these were extracted retrospectively from calendar histories, please say so and describe how. Similarly, fatigue was not among the registered nine-month outcomes. When was the fatigue scale first administered, and is there a pre-treatment baseline?

## 3. A simple accounting check suggests meetings may explain more than 47%

These are rough figures from the published numbers:

- Treated case-processing hours fell by about 4.5 hours a week (12% of 37.9).
- Meeting time fell by about 3.3 hours relative to control (−3.5 against −0.2).
- So **non-meeting hours fell by only about 3%** (from roughly 30.5 to roughly 29.5).
- Output per FTE fell by 3.4%.

That means **output per non-meeting hour was essentially unchanged**. Almost the whole per-hour gain is consistent with removing meeting time from the denominator, rather than with people working faster.

The regression-based mediation estimate (47%) answers a somewhat different question, so the two can differ. But the gap is large enough to discuss, because it bears directly on whether "productivity" rose or low-value time was removed.

It also raises a measurement question. What does "active log-in time" capture? If staff stay logged in during meetings, logs approximate total hours. If logs capture only time spent on cases, an 11% fall in log hours is hard to reconcile with the meeting numbers. Please define the measure precisely.

## 4. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%** on timesheets, with 8.5% on logs at 24 months. The body handles this correctly; the Summary should too.

Similarly, "declined by about a quarter" in §5 is between the like-for-like fall (about 22%) and the mixed-measure fall (about 32%). "About a fifth" on timesheets would be accurate. And per point 1, part of that fall may be the control group improving rather than the treated offices declining.

## 5. Halden follow-up

- **The baseline may be borrowed.** 40.3 hours is exactly the re-analysis's baseline for all 27 time-tracking organisations. Is it the baseline of these 11 organisations? Do all 11 have time tracking, given that only 17 of the 23 record-submitting organisations did? If the baseline belongs to a different set of organisations, the −13.4% and +11.8% figures are unreliable.
- **"Upper bound" isn't justified.** An uncontrolled two-year before-after comparison can be biased in either direction: organisational growth, technology change, staff turnover and changes in product mix could each push the figure up or down. "Not generalisable to organisations in general" is the defensible claim. "Upper bound" is not.
- **There is response selection.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, and the paper doesn't say how responders differ from non-responders. The Summary should note this.
- **"All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the categories.** A marketing agency reverting over *client deadlines* is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. That is mild evidence against a clean coverage/discretionary split, and it should be stated as such rather than absorbed into it.

## 6. Counter arm

- **The early termination is itself informative.** The county ended the counter and contact-centre arm at month 12, effectively a stopping decision driven by an outcome. The waiting-time comparison (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes) is now properly against control, which addresses an earlier gap.
- **The cost figure needs a derivation.** Twelve per cent more staff at full pay suggests cost per contact rises about 12% if contacts handled stay the same. The stated 9% implies more contacts handled or some other offset. Please show the calculation.

## 7. Still missing from the case-processing results

- **Backlog and deadline compliance.** The nine-month report flagged backlogs building up past statutory deadlines as a limitation. It isn't reported at 24 months, though it should be easy to get from the case-management system.
- **Confidence intervals** for the appeal overturn rate, sick days and resignations.
- **Cost per case closed**, including overtime.
- **Sick days per scheduled day.** If 30 hours means four days, a 27% fall is about 9% per scheduled day.

## 8. Section 5: responses to earlier papers

- **The rebuttal of "entirely an artifact" is sound.** It uses records, log hours, randomisation and 24 months, which covers most of the re-analysis's own recommended standards. It would be stronger still once the control-contamination sensitivity check in point 1 is reported. If excluding the two audited offices *raises* the estimate, the rebuttal gets stronger.
- **The rebuttal of "no sign of decay" is effective.** Showing that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours directly undermines the meta-analysis's duration result. Two small points:
  - "The one controlled study with long follow-up" should be checked against the meta-analysis's full list. Some of its 9 controlled studies could have more than 12 months of data that were simply not part of the four.
  - Per point 1, the decline observed here may partly be the control group catching up.

## Overall

The main conclusion is well supported: a real per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years in discretionary public-sector work under rigorous measurement. Most of that gain plausibly comes from removing low-value meeting time. The coverage-bound result is now settled for this employer. The most important revisions are:

1. a sensitivity analysis for the contaminated control offices, and corresponding caution about decay;
2. cluster-appropriate mediation inference, provenance of the baseline meeting and fatigue data, and "supports" instead of "confirms";
3. like-for-like comparisons in the Summary, and checking the Halden subset's baseline.

The unplanned meeting-audit observation also points to the obvious next trial: an arm that reorganises meetings without cutting hours. I can sketch that design or draft revised Summary text if useful.
